competitorScriptHistory.uniqueScript:
Hook: Half the agencies you're jealous of right now are three bad months from closing their doors — and it's not because the market turned on them.

Body: For two years I watched agency owners build businesses that looked incredible from the outside. Beautiful funnels, six-figure launches, screenshots everywhere. But strip away the marketing and there was no actual delivery system underneath — no retention, no fulfillment process, no real client results. Just acquisition dressed up as a business. That works when ad costs are cheap and clients are forgiving. It stops working the second the economy tightens, because tightened budgets expose exactly who was creating value and who was just creating hype. That's what's happening right now. The agencies collapsing aren't collapsing because 'marketing is dead' — they're collapsing because they never built the boring stuff: systems, retention, referrals, a product that keeps working after the sale. The ones surviving are the operators who treated client results like the actual product, not the byproduct.

CTA: If you're not sure which one you are, audit your own retention numbers this week — not your revenue, your retention. That number doesn't lie, and it'll tell you if you're building a real business or a beautiful collapse waiting to happen.

Hook: If your agency made ₹1,00,000 this month and you spent every rupee of it, you don't have a business — you have a job with extra steps.

Why? Because agencies don't die from lack of clients — they die from cash flow gaps. You start taking bad-fit clients. You start discounting your own value because you're scared.

I've watched agency owners scale from one client to fifty, and the ones who survived the dips weren't the most talented — they were the ones who paid themselves this discipline before they paid anything else.

sourceVideo.title: Meta CEO just popped the AI Bubble. like 1999, but worse.
sourceVideo.description:
The AI boom is now driving nearly 50% of all U.S. economic growth, according to Q1 2026 Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) data. And Meta just issued a coy warning that is could all be over soon. 

Spending on AI data centers, Nvidia GPU chips, cloud infrastructure, and hyperscale capital expenditures has exploded over the last two years, making the U.S. economy increasingly dependent on just a handful of technology companies.

One of the biggest developments came from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. After previously saying Meta could rent out AI infrastructure if it ever overbuilt, the company has now begun selling excess AI compute capacity to outside customers. That's a remarkable shift for a company planning to spend up to $150 billion building AI infrastructure. If one of the world's biggest AI investors is already admitting it has excess compute, what does that say about future demand for AI data centers?

We also examine Google's first negative free cash flow quarter since becoming a public company in 2004, Reuters' warning that AI capital expenditures are putting enormous pressure on Big Tech cash flows, and why many of the largest technology companies are now projected to spend more on AI infrastructure than they generate in free cash flow over the next several years.

The implications extend far beyond Silicon Valley. AI capital expenditures now account for nearly 50% of U.S. GDP growth, while consumer spending has remained resilient despite historically low savings rates and stretched household finances. If AI investment begins slowing, it could have major consequences for GDP growth, the stock market, housing market, commercial real estate, employment, and the broader U.S. economy.

Finally, we compare today's market with previous bubbles by examining the S&P 500 CAPE Ratio, stock valuations relative to earnings, and whether today's AI investment boom is beginning to resemble the Dot-Com Bubble of the late 1990s.

In this video:

• AI now accounts for nearly 50% of U.S. GDP growth
• Meta begins selling excess AI compute capacity
• Mark Zuckerberg's warning on AI infrastructure
• Google's first negative free cash flow since 2004
• Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle and Alphabet AI spending
